situation:
You are the finance associate at TIDEGATE TERMINAL SERVICES, a two-year-old port and terminal operator that unloads and stores cargo at a mid-sized river port and runs a small crew hotel on the same property for ship crews waiting between sailings. The managing director (judge) has asked you to recommend how the company should shorten the time between paying its costs and collecting its cash.

The first round of funding leaves about five months of payroll. The company bills shippers forty-five days after a vessel departs, while it pays its stevedores every week and its fuel supplier on delivery, so the cash goes out long before any of it comes back in. The next investor report is due in six weeks.

One course of action is to require payment before cargo leaves the yard and to raise the storage rate charged to ATLAS GULF LINE, the freight line that filled the berths in the first year at a discounted rate when no other carrier would sign. That closes the gap almost at once. It also breaks the terms that line was promised, and it would make the cash figures in the investor report read as an improving business rather than a one-time change in when the company bills.

The other course of action is to hold that rate and those terms and instead delay opening the second floor of the crew hotel, which the seafarers' agency was promised for this winter and for which eleven local residents have already been hired. Delaying it gives up the room revenue that was meant to carry the company through the wait, and it costs the company the staff it hired, who will not wait a year for the work.

The managing director (judge) wants a recommendation on which course of action to take, what the investor report should say about it, and who carries the cost of the choice. The managing director (judge) will greet you, ask to hear your ideas, and will thank you after your presentation and questions.
